name: data.simplex
editorial_article: "data.simplex" is a stark, precise composition by the acclaimed Japanese electronic artist Ryoji Ikeda, appearing as the second track on his highly influential 2005 album, *dataplex*. Released on the seminal German label Raster-Noton, the track exemplifies the album's core aesthetic: the elevation of digital artifacts, binary errors, and clinical sine waves into a form of high-art minimalism. Clocking in at just over one minute, "data.simplex" functions as a sonic study of computational purity, utilizing the interplay of high-frequency blips and meticulously arranged silence to challenge the listener's perception of "music."\n\n*Dataplex* was designed by Ikeda as a deconstruction of data architecture, and "data.simplex" serves as an early, essential pillar in this exploration. By isolating digital noise and stripping away traditional melodic or harmonic structures, Ikeda forces the audience to confront the physical properties of sound. The track is renowned for its extreme clarity and dynamic range, which became a hallmark of Ikeda’s work in the mid-2000s. It stands as a landmark piece of "glitch" and "micro-sound," reflecting an era where the boundary between computer science and musical composition was becoming increasingly porous. For listeners and producers alike, the track remains a testament to the power of extreme reductionism, proving that minimalist textures—when executed with clinical precision—can carry as much emotional and intellectual weight as the most complex orchestral arrangements. It is a quintessential entry in the catalog of contemporary experimental electronics.
